text:
*Interview with Madame Odile Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Madame, I am sorry to keep you up. Please sit down. I need the evening in order, one thing at a time.

MME MONNIER: I remember it, Inspector. Ask what you need.

MATTHEY: Who was at dinner?

MME MONNIER: Dr Vauthier, Monsieur Girard, my nephew Félix, my husband and myself.

MATTHEY: What happened when the temple bell struck nine?

MME MONNIER: My husband made us all show our watches. He does it every year on the last night of the year. He tells each owner what is wrong with his watch.

MATTHEY: And Félix's watch?

MME MONNIER: It showed twenty minutes to nine. My husband scolded him for it. Félix carries his father's silver watch and has never let anyone touch it, my husband included. My husband said so at the table.

MATTHEY: Did anything else pass at dinner that you remember?

MME MONNIER: Monsieur Girard and my husband quarrelled about a price. Monsieur Girard wanted something of my husband's work, and my husband would not sell it at the figure offered. I did not follow the figures. The doctor tried to make them laugh.

MATTHEY: Where did you go afterwards?

MME MONNIER: To the salon. When the temple struck ten I looked at the salon clock. It showed five minutes to ten.

MATTHEY: Who was with you?

MME MONNIER: Dr Vauthier. He has been our friend for thirty years. He is the oldest friend this house has. We played piquet after dinner, without a break.

MATTHEY: When did he leave you?

MME MONNIER: He went out at twenty-eight minutes past ten by the salon clock. He went out to fetch his cigars.

MATTHEY: Did he say anything before he went?

MME MONNIER: He asked me to play for him. I sat down at the piano at once and played until he came back, and I stopped when he came in.

MATTHEY: What did you play?

MME MONNIER: Chopin. He always asks for Chopin, and I always play it for him.

MATTHEY: When he came back, did anything happen?

MME MONNIER: A moment after he came back, the hall clock struck eleven.

MATTHEY: Tell me about your husband, Madame, if you are willing.

MME MONNIER: We have been married thirty years. I was a pastor's daughter, and I knew what I was marrying. I was fond of him. Fondness wears, Inspector, like anything used every day. I do not think that is a thing you wish to hear from a widow.

MATTHEY: And Félix?

MME MONNIER: He owes money. Some of it, I believe, is owed to Monsieur Girard. I do not pretend to know how much. He talks a great deal when he is frightened, and he has been frightened for some time.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you would like to add?

MME MONNIER: Nothing, Inspector. My husband is dead, and I have told you what I know of the evening. I do not intend to weep for you, and I hope you will not expect it.
